newsitem.title: UK: Palladium drops, then rebounds after Russia news.
newsitem.headline: Palladium drops, then rebounds after Russia news.

text.p: The price of palladium, a rare white metal, dropped on Wednesday on news Russia may have signed a long-awaited decree to resume exports halted since December.
In a knee-jerk reaction spot palladium slipped to $153.25 an ounce from a peak of $159.00, losing $2.50 on the day.
The metal, used in electronics and autocatalysts, had gained 42 percent since December as Russia, the world's top supplier, pulled out of the market due to apparent bureaucratic snags.
On Wednesday the deputy director of the export agency for platinum group metals (PGM) Almaz said the decree was signed "in the last few days, although we have not received a copy".
Sergei Gorny said the decree should now prompt the start up of talks with Japan, the world's largest importer, over 1997 contracts.
But precious metals dealers were sceptical about the validity of Russian officials' comments after previous unconfirmed suggestions that exports might resume proved wrong.
"I guess re-wording it (Almaz comments) you could say 'it might not have been signed'," said one London dealer.
But if the decree had been signed, palladium's fortunes untimately clung on how aggressively exports were activated.
"If they come back to the market by doing contract sales with no great catch-up it will take time for prices to correct."
But prices would decline sharply if Almaz sought to catch up the five months of sales it lost with spot PGM offers, he said.
Tony Warwick-Ching, precious markets analyst at CRU International, said the price was unlikely to collapse, as the resumption of sales was to some extent factored in the market.

"We don't know what policies the large funds will follow to offload the stuff. It may not be easy," he added, referring to the U.S.-based Tiger fund which earlier this year admitted being long of palladium on a bullish hunch.
Moreover, Warwick-Ching said, there was little backlog of Japanese imports as they had been shopping around for the metal.
By 1500 GMT prices had trimmed losses with spot palladium quoted at $155.00/$156.00, just 75 cents down from Tuesday.
Its sister metal platinum which, unlike palladium, is more resilient to Russian stoppages as any shorfalls can be filled by the key supplier South Africa, lost $2.25 to trade at $$370.75/$371.75.
Elsewhere in precious metals, gold turned held just above above $340.00 after an initial decline from Tuesday's high of $344.00.
Dealers said physical offtake was likely to keep the market underpinned above $337.50, although chart analysts still reckon a move to test this year's low of $336.15 is on the cards.
